C O M M E N T A R Y

The force awakens, but questions remain: The future of MGUS

​Sæmundur Rögnvaldsson1,2 | Sigurður Yngvi Kristinsson1,2

1Faculty of Medicine, University of Iceland, Reykjavik, Iceland

2Landspítali—­The National University Hospital of Iceland, Reykjavik, Iceland

Correspondence Sæmundur Rögnvaldsson, Faculty of Medicine, University of Iceland, Reykjavik, Iceland. Email: srognvald@hi.is

Commentary on: Stern et al. Investigation and management of the monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS). Br J Haematol 2023;202:734–744.

Keywords: mass spectrometry, MGUS, plasma cell disorders, screening

The emergence of screening for MGUS and mass spectrometry-­based diagnostics could lead to a fundamental shift in the field of plasma cell disorders. Stern and colleagues of the British Society for Haematology present one of the first guidelines discussing these novel ap-proaches and technologies. Questions remain, but the force has awakened…

In their paper Stern et al. present a new British Society of Haematology good practice paper on the investigation and management of monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS). In their paper the authors present a very reasonable approach to both the diagnosis and management of MGUS based on the limited evidence available.1 Interestingly, it is the first clinical recommendation, that we are aware of, to discuss the topic of screening for MGUS. This topic has been gaining interest and we were pleased to see this discussion brought to clinicians and want to com-mend the authors on their level-­headed recommendations. In this commentary, we want to provide our insights on the issue of MGUS screening and the changing landscape of MGUS detection. MGUS was first described by Jan Gösta Waldenström in 1960 when he was experimenting with serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP). He found that M proteins, that he had observed in association with symptomatic multiple myeloma (MM), were sometimes present in individuals who ap-peared healthy.2 We now know that these individuals have a premalignant condition, later termed MGUS and that about 1% of them develop symptomatic MM or related disease per year.3 Observational data have shown that MM patients with prior knowledge of MGUS have better outcomes4,5 and more importantly, recent randomized studies have found that

initiating treatment at the more advanced precursor stage of smouldering MM (SMM) can lead to prevention of symptomatic MM and improves overall survival.6,7 Although early treatment is still debated,8 these data indicate that early treatment can significantly improve outcomes in MM and it is clear that some asymptomatic individuals benefit significantly from early treatment. However, MGUS is usually diagnosed incidentally in individuals who have other med-ical problems and only ~5% of MM patients have a prior diagnosis of MGUS.4 Thus, a vast majority of patients cannot benefit from early treatment. Therefore, the topic of MGUS screening has been gaining increasing attention as it may present a way vastly expanding the availability of early treatment leading to improved outcomes in MM. The extent of these benefits is unclear and more importantly, screening could lead to significant harms. These include, overdiagnosis and overtreatment, potential anxiety and a decreased sense of well-­being in those diagnosed with MGUS, and financial costs and burdens on already strained healthcare systems. As pointed out by Stern and colleagues, robust evidence is therefore needed before recommending the implementation of population-­based screening for MGUS. We are currently conducting the first randomized study evaluating the benefits and harms of MGUS screening, the Iceland screens, treats or prevents MM study (iStopMM).9 iStopMM is a na-tionwide population-­based screening study for MGUS and subsequent randomized controlled trial of follow-­up strategies. A total of 80 759 Icelanders aged above 40 years (54% of the total population) provided informed consent and 75 422 (93%) have been screened by SPEP and free light chain (FLC) assay with immunofixation electrophoresis (IFE) being performed in individual with abnormal results. Those found to have MGUS were randomized to three study arms, arm 1 continues as if they had never been screened, arm 2 is in follow-­up according to current guidelines and arm 3 follows

a more intensive strategy including bone marrow sampling and imaging for all. The primary end point of the study is a difference in overall survival between arm 1 and arms 2 and 3 together with secondary end points of symptomatic MM, MM-­specific survival, and, importantly, quality of life and mental health end points. Early findings show that screening is feasible and that screening leads to increased detection of clinically actionable disease (e.g. early MM and high-­risk SMM).10 Importantly, the study is still and it is still not clear whether this translates into real benefits and what harms are associated with screening. Therefore, it is our view that the recommendations presented, of not to perform MGUS screening at this time, are sensible and in full accordance with the available evidence. However, as data emerge from iStopMM and other non-­randomized studies in the coming years this recommendation may change. If so, screening will fundamentally change the field of MM and related disorders from late intervention to early diagnosis and early intervention, improving survival and quality of life for those affected. The methods of MGUS detection have hitherto mostly relied on the same methodologies used by Dr. Waldenström more than 60 years ago. A recent addition has been the serum FLC assay which indirectly detect monoclonal kappa or lambda FLC as an abnormal ratio of kappa and lambda FLC in the serum. As noted by Stern and colleagues, an abnormal FLC ratio has since been shown to predict risk of MGUS progression and can also be diagnostic of light-­ chain MGUS.1 However, the FLC ratio is not sensitive for MGUS overall and is affected by renal function, and even though recently defined renal reference ranges improve the accuracy of the FLC ratio, it should be used in conjunction with traditional electrophoresis methods at this time.11 In the last few years, a completely new way to detect monoclonal immunoglobulins by mass spectrometry (MS)-­based diagnostics has emerged as a potential replacement to Dr. Waldenström's SPEP. MS measure serum immunoglobulins by mass and charge, lining them onto a spectrum, sim-ilar to SPEP, but with much greater discrimination leading to more accurate and sensitive detection of M proteins.12 This increased sensitivity allows for the detection of much smaller M proteins increasing the prevalence of M proteins from 6% by traditional methods to 41% in one high-­risk cohort in the United States.13 The clinical implications of these smaller M proteins are not clear and further studies are needed. We are currently performing MS as part of the iStopMM study to determine the actual prevalence of small M proteins in the general population, the long-­term per-sistence of these M proteins, and most importantly their clinical implications as predictors of MM and related disorders. Interestingly, MS is included in the good practice paper, as a potential method of tracking low-­level disease at specialized centres.1 In a recent statement, experts of the international myeloma working group state that MS could be used as a replacement of the IFE for more accurate charac-terization of M proteins.12 We think that the recommendations from Stern and colleagues are reasonable at this time and that MS should be performed in specialized centres at

this time. However, the increased accuracy and sensitive detection offered by MS could revolutionize plasma cell disorder diagnostics. As we learn more about how to use this exciting new technology, we would argue that the recommendation presented will most likely change and that MS will become an integral part of MGUS diagnostics and might even replace traditional methods. We feel a growing disturbance in the MGUS force. The combination of population-­based screening and vastly more sensitive diagnostics in the form of MS, is here, a force awak-ening. Together they may fundamentally change the face of MGUS and plasma cell disorders. There remain important questions and we should proceed with optimistic caution and perform clinically relevant studies. That way we can use the force to improve the care of individuals with MGUS, improve outcomes in the disorders it precedes, and most importantly, improve the lives of affected individuals.
